Small villages and towns connected with Highways 
*121. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA : Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the length of roads constructed during the period 1998 to 2003; 
(b) the number of villages and small towns connected with Highways 
through metalled roads during 1998 to 2003; 
(c) whether any study has been conducted to measure progress made, 
consequent upon construction of roads connecting small villages and towns 
with State/National Highways; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KASHIRAM 
RANA): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Since 'Roads' other than National Highways is a State subject 
under the Constitution of India, the Government of India does not maintain 
the data of the length of roads constructed and the number of villages and 
small towns connected through metalled roads. 
However, as a special intervention of the Government of India, the 
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched in December, 
2000 with the aim of providing connectivity to all Unconnected Habitations 
in the rural areas with a population of more than 500 persons, through good 
All-weather roads, by the en d of the Tenth Plan Period . In respect of the Hill 
States (North-East, Sikkim, Him achal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, 
Uttaranchal) Desert Areas and Tribal (S chedule-V) areas, the objective is to 
connect Habitations with a population of 250 persons and above. The

Private coal mining 
*125.   SHRI R.K.ANAND:† 
SHRI ABANI ROY:  
Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring about legislative changes 
allowing private mining while liberalizing norms for allotment of captive 
blocks for trading in coal; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COAL (SHRI KARIYA MUNDA): (a) and (b) A 
Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The Coal Mines (Nationalization) Bill which was introduced in the 
Rajya Sabha on 24-4-2000, seeks to amend the Coal Mines (Nationalization) 
Act, 1973 inter-alia for the following purposes: 
To allow the Indian Companies to (i) mine coal and lignite without the 
existing restriction of captive consumption; (ii) engage in exploration of coal 
and lignite resources in the country. 
As regards allotment of captive blocks, Companies engaged in the 
production of iron and steel, generation of power, manufacture of cement, 
washing of coal obtained from a mine, or such other end-use as the 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri R. K. 
Anancl. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2003] 
Central Government may, by notification specify, are eligible as per the Coal 
Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 as amended in 1993, for captive mining. 
However, since washing of coal obtained from a mine, as an end use, involved 
sale of washed coal in the open market, no coal block for the purpose of 
washing as an end use has been allo cated. This issue has further been 
examined in consultation with the Ministry of Law and Justice and it has been 
decided to allocate blocks for purpose of washing and sale of the washed coal in 
the open market to augment the availability of washed coal to the power, iron and 
steel and cement sector. However, the detailed parameters of the minimum 
capacity, technology, size of the blocks to be allocated and the basis of 
allocation such as competitive bidding an d disposal of the washed coal etc. 
need to be framed before considering requests by companies for allocation of 
coal blocks for above purpose. 
 
Moreover, it has been decided in the Ministry of Coal for allocation of small 
and isolated reserves, which can not be explored scientifically and in an 
economically viable manner, for commercial mining of coal to meet the needs 
of the local industries/populace under the provision of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalization) Act, 1973. The detailed parameters need to be framed before 
the decision is implemented.

(a) whether the Delhi Police had issued circular/instructions that a case of 
dowry can not be registered without inquiry from the Crime Against Women Cell; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the cases registered district wise and year-wise after 1999 without inquiry 
by the Crime Against Women Cell and reasons therefor; and 
(d) the number of cases which had be en registered after 7 years of 
marriage? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI) : (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) No. Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The number of cases registered dist rict-wise, during the period from 
1st January, 2000 to 30th November, 2003 without inquiry by the Crime 
Against Women Cells is given in the Statement I enclosed ( See below). The 
setting up of the Crime Against Women Cell has not diluted the responsibility 
of the local police to initiate action as and when a victim approaches them for 
assistance. Both the Crime Against Women Cell and the local police are 
competent to register and investigate cases of crime against women reported to 
them. 
(d) Delhi Police have during the period from 1 st January, 2003 to 30th 
November, 2003 registered 655 such dowry related cases.

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE) (a) 
to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Government of India have granted enhanced autonomy and 
delegation of powers to Navratna Public Sector Undertakings which includes 
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) for entering into technology 
joint ventures (JVs), to establish financial joint ventures, for opening offices in 
India and abroad, to borrow from international market with the approval of 
RBI and appropriate authorities etc. Accordingly, NTPC is trying to explore 
the business opportunities outside India such as Saudi Arabia, Iran, Oman etc. 
in Power Plant Engineering and Operation and Maintenance of power stations 
through JVs an consortia etc. 
(d) NTPC was incorporated in November, 1975 with the objective of 
planning, promoting and organizing integrated development of thermal power 
in the country. The company has made major contribution to the Power Sector 
development in the country. NTPC's installed capacity as on 31.3.2003 amount 
to 21,249 MW constituting about 19.7% of the country's total installed 
capacity and about 27.7% of the country's total thermal capacity. In 2002-03 
contribution of NTPC is 26.9% of All India Generation and 31.8% of All 
India thermal Generation. NTPC has a committed programme of 
implementing power project with 9370- MW capacity for the Tenth Plan 
period of which 1500 MW has already been commissioned, 4500 MW is on-
going; and proposals for 3370 MW are at various stages of progress. 
Further, NTPC has adopted a Corporate Plan to become a 40,000 MW 
plus company by the year 2012 and NTPC is making all endeavours to realize 
this target. NTPC has also entered in to Hydro power sector with 800 MW 
Koldam Hydro Electric Project in Himachal Pradesh.

*130. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR : Will the Minister of POWER be

(a) whether the power Grid Corporation of India has drawn up guidelines 
for the States overdrawing their requirements of power when the system

collapse; and 
(c) whether the guidelines will prove a deterrent against overdrawal and 
ensure grid discipline? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): 
(a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Central Elecrticity Regulatory Commission (CERC) has apprpved the 
Indian Electricity Grid Code (IEGC) vide its order dated 30th October, 1999 
According, IEGC was issued by Central Transmission Utility i.e.

POWERGRID in discharge of its statutory duties which came into effect from 1 
st February, 2000. The lEGC lays down the rules, guidelines and standards to 
be followed by the various constituents in the system to plan, develop, maintain 
and operate the power system in the most efficient reliable and economic manner. 
According to the provisions of lEGC, all regional constituents should make all 
possible efforts to ensure that the grid frequency always remains within the 49.0 
to 50.5 Hz. Band. Further, when the frequency falls below 49.0 Hz. requisite load

Electricity Act, 2003 for issuing directions as well as for levying penalty on

regime also provides commercial deterrent against overdrawal by the utilities.

*139. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

said problems of rural population of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KASHIRAM 
RANA): (a) to (c) The Ministry of  Rural Development is presently 
implementing the following major schemes for poverty alleviation, 
employment generation, area development and infrastructure development in the 
rural areas of the country: 
• Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) 
• Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) 
• Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) 
• Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) 
• Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) 
• Watershed Development Programmes (IWDP, DPAP and DDP) and 
• Central Rural Sanitation Programme (CRSP) 
The SGSY and the SGRY are the major employment generating schemes 
for the rural poor. The Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) and the Watershed 
Development Programmes (IWDP, DPAP and DDP) also create employment 
indirectly in the rural areas. 
2. The Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozga r Yojana (SGSY) is the major on-
going programme for the self-employment of rural poor. The objective of the 
SGSY is to bring the assisted Swarozgaris above the poverty line by providing 
them income-generating assets through bank credit and Government subsidy. 
Under the SGRY, additional wage employment

and economic assets for sustained employment and development. Provision 
of food security is another objective of  the scheme. These schemes are to be

empowering them. The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) seeks 
to provide connectivity to all unconnected habitations in the rural areas with a 
population of more than 500 persons with good all-weather roads by the end 
of the Tenth Five-Year Plan. Th e Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP) is being implemented to provide safe drinking water in 
rural areas. With a view to widening the coverage of rural sanitation, a Total 
Sanitation Campaign (TSC) is now being implemented in Project Mode in the 
identified districts. The Integrated  Wastelands Development Programme 
(IWDP) is implemented to improve the productivity of the Wastelands and 
living standard of the rural poor. 
3. The Ministry constantly reviews its programmes for policy 
interventions for improvement of the schemes. Erstwhile Integrated Rural 
Development Programme (IRDP) and allied programmes, namely, Training 
of Rural Youth for Self Employment (TRYSEM), Development of Women 
and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Supply of Improved Toolkits to 
Rural Artisans (SITRA), Ganga Kalyan Yojana (GKY) and Million Wells 
Scheme (MWS) were restructured into a single self-employment programme 
namely, Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) from 1st April, 1999. 
A new wage employment programme, namely, the Sampoorna Grameen 
Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) was introduced w.e.f. 25-09-2001 after merging the 
erstwhile Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) and the Jawahar Gram

Prevention of" Atrocities Act, 1989 for SCs and STs both in letter 
and spirit. 
(b) Identification of atrocities • prone areas, preparing action plans and 
taking necessary preventive steps to  protect the life and property of 
the members of the SCs and STs in these areas. 
(c) Sensitise the police personnel to have a more sympathetic approach 
while dealing with cases of atrocities against SCs and STs, 
 
(d) Recruitment of sufficient number of persons belonging to SCs and 
STs in police force especially at the cutting edge level. 
(e) Setting up of special cells to deal with offences against SCs and STs 
and evaluate their working to ensure speedy disposal of pending 
cases with the Police. 
(f) Setting up special courts to reduce the pendency of such cases and to 
improve the rate of conviction by courts. Devise measures/ strategies to 
improve the rate of conviction, which could include adequate 
incentives to witnesses to appear in the courts. 
(g) Development programmes for creating awareness among the 
vulnercble sections of society and legal recourse open to them. 
(h) Implement schemes and development programmes for empowering 
the members of the SC and ST communities. 
As a result of the above advisories, the States and Union Territories have taken 
the following actions: 
(a) Special Cells have been set up in  the States/UTs of Andhra Pradesh, 
Bihar, Chhatisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Punjab, 
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal and Pondicherry 
toward implementation of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled

Sexual harassment of women at their work place 
844. DR. AKHILESH DAS : Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the context of ever increasing incidence of rapes and other 
related crimes against women, Government have called for a review about 
implementation of the Supreme Court's directions for prevention of harassment 
and sexual abuse of women at place of work in different States and Union 
Territories; 
(b) what guidelines were issued by the Apex Court in this regard; 
(c) what steps have been taken by the Central and State Governments to 
enforce the same; and 
(d) the number of cases of each type of abuse against women at place of 
work in each State and Union Territory since issue of guidelines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) A Central Committee headed by Secretary, 
Department of Women and Child Devel opment has been constituted in the 
Department of Women and Child Development to monitor the 
implementation of the guidelines laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court to 
prevent sexual harassment of women at their work place. 
(b)and (c)The guidelines and norms laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
and initiatives taken by the Government are at Statements I & II respectively. 
(See below) 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2003 ] 
(d) The Government does not receive co mplaints directly as these are to 
be dealt with by the Complaints Committees formed in various 
Ministries/Departments. 
Statement-I 
Guidelines and norms laid down by the Hon 'ble Supreme Court in Vishaka 
& Ors. v. State of Rajasthan & Ors. [JT1997(7) SC 384] 
HAVING REGARD to the definition of 'human rights' in Section 2(d) 
of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, Taking note of the fact 
that the present civil and penal laws in India do not adequately 
provide for specific protection of women from sexual harassment in 
work places and that enactm ent of such legislation w ill take 
considerable time. 
It is necessary and expedient for employers in work places as well as 
other responsible persons or institutions to observe certain guidelines 
to ensure the prevention of sexual harassment of women. 
1. Duty of the Employer or other responsible persons in work 
places and other institutions: 
It shall be the duty of the employer or other responsible persons in 
work places or other institutions to  prevent or defer the commission 
of acts of sexual harassment and to provide the procedures for the 
resolution, settlement or prosecution of acts of sexual harassment by 
taking all steps required. 
2. Definition : 
For this purpose, sexual harassment includes such unwelcome sexually 
determined behaviour (whether directly or by implication) as: 
(a) Physical contact and advances; 
(b) a demand or request for sexual favours; 
(c) sexually coloured remarks; 
94 

[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) showing pornography; 
(e) any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of 
sexual nature. 
Where any of these acts is commit ted in circumstances where-under 
the victim of such conduct has a reasonable apprehension that in relation 
to the victim's employment or work whether she is drawing salary, or 
honorarium or voluntary, whether in Government, public or private 
enterprise such conduct can be humiliating and may constitute a health 
and safety problem. It is discriminatory for instance when the woman 
has reasonable grounds to believe that her objection would disadvantage 
her in connection with her employment or work including recruiting or 
promotion or when it creates a hostile work environment. Adverse 
consequences might be visited if the victim does not consent to the 
conduct in question or raises any objection thereto. 
3.   Preventive steps: 
All employers or persons in charge  of work place whether in public 
or private sector should take appropriate steps to prevent sexual 
harassment. Without prejudice to the generality of this obligation 
they should take the following steps: 
(a) Express prohibition of sexual harassment as defined above at the 
work place should be notified, published and circulated in 
appropriate ways. 
(b) The Rules/Regulations of Government and Public Sector 
bodies relating to conduct and discipline should include 
rules/regulation prohibiting sexual harassment and provide for 
appropriate penalities in such rules against the offender. 
(c) As regard private employers steps should be taken to include 
the aforesaid prohibitions in the standing order under the Industrial 
Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. 
(d) Appropriate work conditions should be provided in repsect of 
work, leisure, health and hygiene to further ensure that there is 
no hostile environment towards women at work pl aces and no 
employee woman should have reasonable gr ounds to believe 
that she is disadvantaged in connection with her employment. 
95 

RAJYASABHA [10 December, 2003] 
Criminal Proceedings: 
Where such conduct amounts to a specific offence under the Indian 
Penal Code or under any other law, the employer shall initiate 
appropriate action in accordance with law by making a complaint 
with the appropriate authority. 
In particular, it should ensure that victims or witnesses are not 
victimized or discriminated against while dealing with complaints of 
sexual harassment. The victims of sexual harassment should have the 
option to seek transfer of the perpetrator or their own transfer. 
5.   Disciplinary Action: 
Where such conduct amounts to misconduct in employment as 
defined by the relevant service rules, appropriate disciplinary action 
should be initiated by the employer in accordance with those rules. 
&   Complaint Mechanism: 
Whether or not such conduct constitutes an offence under law or a 
breach of the service rules, an appropriate complaint mechanism should 
be created in the employer's organization for redress of the complaint 
made by the victim. Such complaint mechanism should ensure time 
bound treatment of complaints. 
7.   Complaints Committee: 
The complaint mechanism, referred to in (6) above, should be 
adequate to provide, where nece ssary, a Complaints Committee, a 
special counsellor or other s upport service including the 
maintenance of confidentiality. 
The Complaints Committee should be headed by a woman and not 
less than half of its member should be women. Further to prevent 
the possibility of any undue pressure or influence from senior levels, 
such Complaints Committee should involve a third party, either NGO 
or other body who is familiar with the issue of sexual harassment. 
The Complaints Committee must make an annual report to the 
Government department concerned of the complaints and action taken 
by them. 
96 

[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The employers and persons in charge will also report on the compliance 
with the aforesid guidelines including on the reports of the Complaints 
Committee to the Government department. 
8. Workers' Initiative: 
Employees should be allowed to raise issues of sexual harassment at 
workers' meeting and in other appropriate forum and it should be affirmatively 
discussed in Employer/Employee Meetings. 
9. Awareness: 
Awareness of the rights of female employees in this regard should be created in 
particular by prominently notifying the guidelines (and appropriate 
legislation when enacted on the subject) in a suitable manner. 
10. Third Party Harassment: 
Where sexual harassment occurs as a result of an act or omission by any third party 
or outsider, the employer and person in charge will take all steps necessary and 
reasonable to assist the affected person in terms of support and preventive 
action. 
11. The Central/State Governments are requested to consider adopting 
suitable measures including legislation to ensure that the guidelines laid down 
by this order are also observed by the employers in Private Sector. 
12. These guidelines will not prejudice any rights available under the Protection of 
Human Right Act, 1993.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRII.D.SWAMI):(a)YesSir. 
(b) The Government have recentely revised the Scheme for 
Modernization of State Police Forces (MPF Scheme). The revised scheme has 
grouped the State into 3 categories. A, Bl and B2-mainly on the basis of level 
of insurgency/militancy/cross border terrorism being faced by the State.

these three categories of States respectively from 2003-04. The Central 
funding will be in the form of grant-in-aid. As a 
100 

[December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
result, the annual Central allocation has been raised from Rs. 1000 crore to Rs.

Sikkim, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. 
Category B2: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, 
Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, 
Goa, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala Tamil Nadu.

Scheme for Reimbursement of Security Related Expenditure (SRE) operated 
by the Internal Security Division of Ministry of Home Affairs have been 
merged with the MPF Scheme. Central funding for which will be 100% in 
respect of the Left-wing Extremist (LWE) affected districts of the concerned 
States, irrespective of whether the States fall in category A, Bl or B2 within the 
overall control assistance for these States. 
The Scheme for Modernization of Stat e Police Forces of the North East 
Division under which assistance was given in kind, as well as the items for 
police modernization inducted under the SRE Scheme of the Department of 
Jammy& Kashmir have also been merged with the MPF Schema from 2003-
04.

Processing waste to produce power 
859. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that large amounts of garbage is dumped every-day 
and also sometimes it gets piled up in the colonies polluting, the areas; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to process the waste garbage and 
produce electricity and biogas; 
(c) now many such plants are existing in various cities across the 
country; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to encourage this? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) 
The biodegradable and combustible components segregated from the garbage 
being dumped in the colonies, which may pollute the areas in the absence of 
proper collection and disposal methods, can be processed for production of 
biogas and electricity through processes such as bio-methanation, combustion, 
pyrolysis, gasification, etc. The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources 
is implementing a National Programme on Energy Recovery from Urban and 
Industrial Wastes to promote setting up of projects to process the garbage and 
industrial wastes for recovery of energy/generation of electricity. 
(c) Under the above National Programme, three projects for generation 
of energy have been installed so far in the country at Hyderabad and 
Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh and Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh. 
(d) The Ministry's scheme on Energy Recovery from Urban and 
Industrial Wastes provides for various fiscal and financial incentives for 
setting up wastes to energy projects. The scheme has been made 
applicable to private as well as  public sector entrepreneurs and 
organizations including Non-Governmental Organizations who may set 
up waste to energy projects on the basis of Build, Own and Operate 
(BOO), Build Own Operate and Transfer (BOOT) Build Operate and Transfer 
(BOT) and Build Operate Lease and Tr ansfer (BOLT). The states have 
been requested to declare policy guidelines for facilitating the promoters 
120 

[ 10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
to set up waste to energy projects in th eir states and ten states have already 
declared the policy. Further, the Mu nicipal Solid Wastes (Management and 
Handling) Rules, 2000 notified by the Ministry of Environment and Forests, 
Government of India has laid down standards for processing or disposal 
facilities which includes energy recovery.

860. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : Will the Minister ot NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that the Gujarat Energy Development Agency 
(GEDA) is using fruit and vegetable waste to generate electricity; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the demonstration plant Naroda Gl DC, 
generates about 130 units of electricity everyday out of one tonne of 
foodwaste; and 
(c) if so, the efforts the Government plan to make to encourage the use of 
foodwaste to generate energy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) and (b) 
The Gujarat Energy Development Agen cy (GEDA), Vadodara has installed a 
Biogas Plant of 85 cubic metre gas production per day capacity based on agro-
food processing industrial wastes for generation of electricity at GIDC 
Naroda, Ahmedabad. The plant has been designed to treat about 2 tonnes of 
wastes per day and is generating about 120-130 units of electricity every day. 
(c) GEDA has informed that a proposal was under their consideration to 
extend financial support for such projects. The Ministry of Non-Conventional 
Energy Sources is implementing a Nati onal Programme on Energy Recovery 
from urban and industrial wastes to promote setting up of projects for generation 
of energy/power from urban and industrial wastes including wastes from fruits and 
vegetable markets as well as processing industries with minimum installed 
capacity of 300 cubic meter biogas per day/25KW. The programme provides 
for fiscal and financial incentives for setting up waste to energy projects. Two 
demonstration projects for generation of electricity from vegetable market 
wastes are under installation at Vijayawada (Andhra Pradesh) and Chennai 
(Tamil Nadu), in addition to the plant at Naroda, Ahmedabad.

Guidelines of the CERC for power sector 
875. SHRI ABANI ROY : Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Central Electricit y Regulatory Commission has recently 
announced guidelines and enablin g procedures for open access in 
transmission in the power sector; 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2003] 
(b) if 50, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the distribution companies and trading companies would be 
benefited by the guidelines of the CERC; and 
(d) if so, to what extent? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SH'RIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) The Central Electricity Regulatory 
Commission (CERC) has issued an orde r on open access in the inter-State 
transmission on 14.11.2003. The CERC has also issued the draft regulation on 
terms and condition of open access inters tate transmission on 3.12.2003 for 
suggestions and comments from the interested parties. The CERC draft 
regulation provides that all transmission service providers in the country 
including POWERGRID shall provide non-discriminatory open access for inter-
State transmission to any distribution company, trader, generating company, 
captive plant or any permitted consumer  with immediate e ffect. Apart from 
creating new options for distribution companies and bulk customers for 
buying power, this will facilitate completion in the power generation industry. 
The salient features of the order are at Statement. 
Statement 
Salient Features of CERC's order on open access in inter-state 
transmission 
* Existing Regional Postage Stamp pricing method is to be applied. 
* Discoms, Traders, IPPS, captive Plants can immediately^avail inter-
State open access. 
* Two categories of open access customers-short term and long term. 
* Nodal Agency for short term customers will be the RLDC within 
which the point of drawal is located. 
* CTU will be the nodal agency for long term customers. 
* Minimum 5 years commitment required for becoming long term 
customer. 
* Long term customers to be treated at par with original beneficiaries 
of the CTU network. 
* Short term customers will be curtailed first in case of transmission 
constraint. 
140 

[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
* Mismatches in the energy drawals by the open access customers to be 
billed as per the existing frequency linked unscheduled interchange 
charges under Availability Based Tariff (ABT) 
* CERC recommends adoption of ABT at the State level. 
Mega power policy 
876. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to announce the new tariff regulations and 
trading policy for the power sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) by when, these are expected to be made operational; 
(d) whether Government also propose to carry out a comprehensive change 
in the mega power policy; and 
(e) if so, the details of the proposed amendments? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (e) Section 3(1) of the Electricity 
Act, 2003 provides inter alia that the Central Govern ment shall prepare the 
National Electricity Policy and tariff policy in consultation with the State 
Governments and the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). Views of the State 
Governments have been solicited on formulation of these policies. A 
preliminary discussion paper on tariff policy was prepared with the assistance 
of CEA and Credit Rating Information Services of India Ltd. (CRISIL.) and 
circulated to all the State Governments for their comments and suggestions. 
Since the Policies are of vital importance for the smooth development of the 
power sector, the Government of India has constituted a Task Force on Power 
Sector Investments and Reforms under the chairmanship of Shri N.K. Singh, 
Member (Energy), Planning Commission, with the terms of reference inter 
alia, to recommend an Electricity Tariff Policy and also to evolve and 
recommend a National Electricity Policy. 
The State Governments have been requested to give their views on the 
terms of reference of the Task Force. The Task Force also held a meeting with 
Energy/Power Secretaries of States on 4th December, 2003. Meetings have also 
been held with other stakeholders. The Task Force is deliberating on the issues 
involved.

generating company intending to set up a hydro generating station shall 
prepare and submit to the Authority for its concurrence, a scheme estimated to

Planning Commission has delegated full powers to State Governments for

Power to all by 2012 
881. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY : Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state : 
(a) whether the Prime Minister's vision of providing power to all by 
2012 seems to be very difficult to achieve; 
(b) if so, whether there is a need  to cut duty on power equipment 
imports; 
(c) whether according to estimates, the current burden of accumulated losses 
on the States are over Rs.3,00,000 crores; 
 
(d) if so, whether the Electricity Act, 2003 was formulated to rationalize 
the tariff structure by bringing in competitive environment; 
(e) if so, what are the other difficulties that are being faced to implement 
the Prime Minister's vision of power to all by 2012; and 
(f) to what extent these hurdles have been removed? 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Providing power to all by 2012 is an ambitious but 
achievable goal. 
(b) There is a provision for duty free import of equipment and deemed 
export benefits for mega power projects. 
(c) According to Central Electricity Authority (CEA) the estimated 
accumulated losses based on data available form the state were 28999.002 
crores for the year 2001-02 (Provisional), Rs. 20262.26 crores for the year 2002-
03 (Revised Estimates). 
(d) The Electricity Act, 2003 has been  enacted with th e objective of, 
inter-alia, taking measures conducive to development of electricity industry, 
promoting competition therein, rationalization of electricity tariff and 
ensuring transparent policies regarding subsidies. 
(e) and (f) In order to provide "power to all by 2012", the Central 
Electricity Authority (CEA) has estimated the requirement of an additional 
capacity of about 1,00,000 MW. For th e 10th Five Year Plan, a capacity 
addition target of approximately 41,000 MW has been fixed. In addition to 
this, about 3000 MW is likely to come from renewables. 
The strategy of power sector reforms focusing on distribution combined with 
step-up in public sector investment in generation in the 10th Plan aims at a 
qualitative transformation of the power sector. To address the problem of poor 
sub-transmission and distribution systems, the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) is being implemented with a 
budget provision of Rs. 3500 crore in 2003-04 for financing specific projects in 
distribution circles and for providing grants as incentive for reducing cash 
losses by SEBs/State Utilities. 
In addition, priority is being given to : 
o  Improvement of Plan Load Factor (PLF) of the existing power 
stations.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Government of India (GOI) counter 
guarantee scheme for power projects was developed as a transitory measure to 
boost private investment and it was decided in 1994 to extend counter guarantee 
to 8 initial projects cleared for making foreign investment in the power sector. 
It was also decided that the GOI counter guarantee would not be extended to any 
more power projects. 
Government has accordingly issued counter guarantee to six of the projects 
viz., 740 MW Dabhol (Phase-I) and 1082 MW Bhadrawati power projects in 
Maharashtra, 216 MW Jegurupadu (P hase-I) and 1040 MW Visakhapatnam

lapsed due to inability of the projects to comply with the required conditions. 
Promoters of the Godavari project in Andhra Pradesh withdrew the request for a 
GOI counter guarantee. 
Counter guarantee to the Mangalore pr oject in Karnataka as also fresh 
counter guarantee to the lb Valley project could not be issued since the 
respective State Governments did not accept the prescribed conditions. The 
promoters of these two projects have since left and it has been decided to 
withdraw the offer for counter guarantee. 
Three of the projects with counter guarantee viz. Dabhol (Phase-I), 
Jegurupadu (Phase-I) and Neyveli-Zero Unit have been commissioned.

Installation of faulty electronic meters in Delhi 
887. SHRI RAMADHAR KASHYAP: Will the Minsiter of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the attention of the Government has been drawn to the news 
items titled "DERC question meter norms" appearing in the media; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; 
(c) whether Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) has conducted field 
surveys and found that most of the el ectronic meters installed in Delhi are 
running too fast; and 
(d) if so, the names of the companies who have supplied these meters and what 
action the Commission has taken to replace these faulty meters? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA):(a)and(b)Yes, Sir. Delhi Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (DERC) has statutory duty to specify and enforce 
standards with respect to quality, continuity and reliability of services 
provided by licensees. 
(c) and (d) Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) has set up a 
committee to look into the various complaints received from the consumers in 
connection with their electricity meters. The Committee which undertook 
testing of about 375 meters has observed that more than 91% of the meters so 
tested recorded consumption level whic h were within the prescribed limit 
given in the Indian Electricity Rules. About 2% of the meters were found to be 
slow and 0.5% were faster than the prescribed limit. About 5% of the meters, 
however, were found to be defective. The findings of the committee were 
published through a Press Note by Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(DERC). These recommendations are Annexed. 
Subsequent to the issue of press replease Commission has also tested 
about 38 meters. Out of these 6 elect ronic meters replaced by distribution 
companies and 4 electromechanical meters installed during Delhi Vidyut Board 
period were found to be fast and one meter was found to be slow beyond the 
specified limit. DERC at present is looking into the procedure/norsm for testing 
of meters. 
Distribution companies have been advised by DERC to take necessary 
action on the line of these recommendations. 
158 

 
[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Recommendations of the Committee set up by DERC 
* The performance of M/s TTL meters, wherever installed, should be 
monitored by the DISCOMs concerned and be replaced wherever 
any defect is noticed. 
* The BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. (BRPL) should not install any TTL 
meters until the design defects found in these meters are rectified to 
the satisfaction of the BRPL. The modified meters should be sample 
tested by the above Committee before installation. 
* Meters of Elymer procured by the erstwhile DVB are also found to be 
sub-standard. These meters are electro-magnetic type and the DISCOM 
would consider changing them on priority. 
* In cases where the consumers are of  the view that their meters are 
ruuning fast, they may take up such cases with the DISCOMs for testing 
of their meters in accordance with DERC (Performance Standard-
Metering & Billing) Regulations. 
* Wherever the consumers find a quantum jump in their consumption 
(recorded by digital meters), they may report the matter to the 
DISCOMs. The DISCOM shall replace the meter and billing for the 
period shall be done in accordance with DERC (Performance Standard-
Metering & Billing) Regulation.

915. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of RURAL

188 

[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether it is a fact that only 4.59 per cent of the total BPL families 
were covered during 1999—2002 under Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar 
Yojana (SGSY) and as a result of this th e target of covering of at least 30 per 
cent of the BPL families under the scheme in five years also appears 
unrealizable; 
(b) if so, the reasons for the poor coverage of the scheme between 1999-
2002; 
(c) the state which were lagging in the implementation of the Scheme; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the funding pettern of the SGSY i.e. in the 
ratio 75:25 by the Centre and the State, was not stricitly followed and there 
was a significant shortfall in the release of matching funds in several States; 
(e) whether there were large scale diversions, misutilisation and parking 
of funds curtailing the actual funding for the programme in several States; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI U. V. KRISHNAM RAJU): (a) and (b) Coverage of 
Below Poverty Line families during initial years of implementation of 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (S GSY) was slow and it was expected 
as it is a process oriented scheme and has adopted a new concept of group 
approach. In the guidelines of SGSY it was mentioned that the effort should be 
to see that broadly 30% of the rural poor in the block are covered during the 
next five years. However this was subject to availability of funds. 
Subsequently this provision has been deleted during the course of amendments 
to the guidelines of the SGSY because the availability of funds has not been 
comparable and also because the target oriented approach has been given up so 
as to have qualitative improvement in the implementation of the programme. 
The reasons for low coverage during initial years was due to the fact that during 
the first and second year of implementation of the scheme much of the time was 
utilized for training and sensitization of development functionaries and banks 
officials, constitution of committees at  various levels, identification of key 
activities, preparation of project reports, social mobilization for formation of 
Self Help Groups and training of SHGs etc. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2003]

the funds available in the States of Bi har, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh and West

month of date of sanction of central releases. During the course of the 
performance review meeting it was noticed that a few states were not 
releasing their contribution in time. On ascertaining the reasons from the State 
Governments, it was observed that significant delay was due of budgetary 
constraint. Some North Eastern States like Assam and Manipur could not release 
their matching share. The reasons for sh ort release to State share is due to 
enhancement of allocation by the Government of India so as to provide 10% of 
total resources for the North Eastern States. As a result, the State Matching Share

weak financial position.

Problem of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, sexual harassment of 
women at workplace is increasing at an alarming rate. Over sixty per cent of 
working women have been victims of male malice and molestation. But due 
to shame, social stigma and for fear of  reprisal, women have silently suffered 
this menace. Only 5 to 6 per cent of such incidents are reported and only a 
few culprits are punished. 
According to a report of the Nati onal Crime Records Bureau, sexual 
harassment of women has increased from 5671 reported cases in 1996 to 
8123 in 1998. It is an in crease of over 40 per cent in  just two years. No other 
crime has increased at such an alarming rate. 
These statistics perhaps have taken into account, only the cases of 
working women in the organised sector. What about women in the 
unorganised sectors like construction workers, brick-kiln workers, farm 
labourers, etc.? 
The National Commission for Women has already drafted the Sexual 
Harassment (Prevention and Redress) Bill, 2003 for enactment into a law by 
Parliament, but Government is yet to examine this and bring before 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2003] 
Parliament. Gender bias is one of the major factors and thus harassment of women 
remains an insidious reality. 
I make an earnest appeal to the Government to examine the said Bill 
anew and introduce the same in Parliament during the current Session and also to all 
the hon. Members of the august House to rise above party lines and lend their 
support for passage of the Bill when it comes before the House for consideration, 
which is in the news for the last three years.

Regarding the Resignation of Shri Dilip Singh Judev, Minister of State in the Ministry 
of Environment and Forests from the Council of Ministers 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, the Delhi edition of The Indian Express dated 16th November, 2003, 
carried a news story and VCD visuals, allegedly showing Shri Dilip Singh Judev, 
then Union Minister of State for Environment and Forests, receiving cash from one 
Shri Rahul in the presence of Shri Natwar Rateria, Assistant Private Secretary to the 
Minister. Shri Dilip Singh Judev submitted his resignation which was accepted by 
the President on my recommendation on 17th November, 2003. On my direction, the 
Cabinet Secretariat forwarded on 17th November, 2003, press clippings from various 
newspapers to the CBI for appropriate action. 
On the basis of the above Indian Express news story and other print and 
electronic media reports, the CBI registered a preliminary case on 18th November, 
2003 against Shri Judev, his APS Shri Natwar Rateria, and Shri Rahul, purportedly a 
representative of an Australian mining company. 
The decision to register a Preliminary Enquiry or a regular case or file a 
chargesheet is a decision taken by the CBI. The Government does not interfere 
in these decisions. 
The CBI has also sent notices to both Shri Judev and Shri Rateria requiring 
them to appear before the CBI. 
222 

[10 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
It has been the policy of my Government that all allegations 
pertaining to corruption should be thoroughly inquired into. Accordingly, the 
CBI is inquiring into this whole matter and it would be premature to state 
anything till the inquiry is complete. 
As Hon. Members are aware, th e CBI has full functional autonomy 
and, under the recently enacted Ce ntral Vigilance Commission Act, the 
superintendence of the CBI in relation to offences under the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, has been vested by the Government in the Central Vigilance 
Commission. 
There should, therefore, be no fear or misgiving regarding the 
independence of this inquiry. 
I would like to assure this august House that the truth will soon be 
out and the law will take its own course.  Thank you.

MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Hon. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would like 
to say a few things for the consideration of the hon. Minister for Human Resource 
Development who has presented the National Charter for Children, 2003. This is a well

National Agenda for Governance adopted by the National Democratic Alliance 
Government in 1999. 
Now, I would like to express my views in Oriya. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman Sir, I would like to express my profuse thanks to the 
Hon'ble Minister of Human Resource Development for having brought the 
National Charter for children, 2003. This is a very well thought out and elaborately 
drafted document. This document is in part fulfilment of the national agenda for 
governance adopted by N.D.A Government in 1999. Now I would like to continue 
my speech in Oriya to express my views on the motion. 
Sir, there are many provisions "incorporated in our Constitution for the 
development of women and children. There are also certain constitutional 
provisions for the development and welfare of the children in our society. The 
relevant articles of the Constitution are Art. 15.3, Art. 24, Art. 39 Art. 51. In 
Article 24 of the Constitution, it has been prohibited to engage children below 14 
years of age, in industries and mines as labourers.   But it has not been clearly 
stated whether the children can be

engaged as labourers in other sectors.  Everywhere we come across children 
below the age 14 engaged as domestic servants. The number of child 
labourers employed in small hotels and tea-shops is the maximum. 
There is an urgent need to rescue the child labourers and rehabilitate 
them properly by providing proper education and social security. It has also 
been found that such parents who live on begging also force their children to 
be beggars. There is a need to rehabilita te these street beggars, otherwise in 
their later lives they will indulge themselves in bigger anti-social activities. It 
is not always true that only children of  poor families are neglected. It has also 
been found that children of well-to-do fa milies are also misguided due to lack 
of proper education and guidance. This results in disharmony in the society. 
The first victim of advanced Medical Science is female foetus. A female child 
is unwanted in the society due to the prevailing social evils like dowry. 
Parents shy away from spending money on female child, on her education and 
health care. If we really want to save future mothers of our country then there 
is a need to provide equal opportunity and protection to both the male and 
female child. Education is the fundamenta l right of everybody in the society. 
Proper environment and education each required for the allround development 
of a child. Education makes him cultured and develops his personality. 
Sir, education can only ensure a progressive and healthy society in 
our country. The purpose of educatio n is character building. There is 
disharmony in the society, because we have all been misguided and have lost 
direction at some point of time. As the life of a building depends upon the 
strength of its foundation, similarly the future of the country depends upon its 
children. Children are the future of the country. If we want them to be good 
citizens we should provide them with good upbringing and guide them on the 
right path. The parents and teachers have a greater responsibility in providing 
proper upbringing to the children. The children should grow in the right kind 
of environment not only in their homes but also in schools. Home is the first 
school of a child and the mother is the first teacher. The child gets influenced 
by the mother, father and other member s of the family, and the society as a 
whole, but knowingly or unknowingly the child grows under the maximum 
influence of the mother. Therefore the mother should be the embodiment of 
all the good qualities. Mother plays a dominant role for the spiritual and moral 
development in the personality of a child. Only a mother can guide the child 
properly. The school is the second ho me where the character and intellectual 
development

SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN (Karnataka): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I 
welcome these two Bills introduced by the hon. Railway Minister, that is, the 
Railway (Second Amendment) Bill, 2003 and the Railway Protection Force 
(Amendment) Bill, 2003. The hon. Minister has just now explained the 
provision for these two Bills, that is, to give more powers to the Railway 
Protection Force. The Railway Protecti on Force, as the hon. Minister has 
rightly said, has about 70,000 personnel. They were having all the capabilities 
of a police force or a disciplined force, but they had no powers. They were 
like watch and ward so far. They were having guns but they have no right to 
use the guns. They detect certain frauds and crimes, but they have no power to 
prosecute immediately. They will have to hand over such criminals to the 
State police force, under the law. It is a very peculiar situation that a person, 
who detects a crime, will have no power to prosecute. This has been talked 
about for a very long time, as I remember. We have debated this issue in the 
Parliament also why such a power of trying and prosecution of crimes, which

Budgetary support being provided for this purpose. Have you got any plan for 
this? Sir, I hope the hon. Minister would enlighten us on this when he replies. 
Then, in the definitions, along with railway properties, you have added 
'passenger area' and 'passengers' as well. But Section 3 has remained the same. 
You don't want to amend this Section. Section 3 states and I quote: "There 
shall be constituted and maintained by the Central Government to be called the 
Railway Protection Force for the better protection and security of the railway 
property." Even after the amendment, it is going to remain the same, which 
means that the passenger area and passengers are not going to be included. 
Why is it that this has been left out? I would like to know whether the Law 
Department had approved this, or, is there a lacuna? I hope the hon. Minister 
would clarify as to why he does not want to add 'passenger area' and 'passengers' 
under Section 3. 
Then, as the railway employees, they are going to take up inquiry as well 
as prosecutions in their hands. Now, when the judicial power is at the hands of the 
executive, say, the police officers, in case of a conflict between the two, namely, 
the police and the RPF, what is the mechanism you have to resolve this conflict? 
Then, as regards the Railway Protection Force Act itself, according to 
Section 10 of the Act, they are deemed to be railway employees. Then, according to 
Sections nine (9) and seventeeen (17) of the Act, they can be punished by the higher 
authorities. And, according to Section 15 (a), they don't have the power to form 
associations. I agree with that because the Armed Forces cannot join hands with 
labour. But they are being protected under article 311 of the Indian Constitution.   If 
they have protection as per

SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL (Haryana): Sir, in fact, the suggestions should 
have been taken up first. I wanted to speak on this Bill, and I gave my name much

Members of Parliament. Sir, one very good thing about the Indian Railways is the

about a very important person, namely, the railway passenger. So, in that respect, I 
thank the hon. Minister. But, my difficulty is that the legislation is incomplete on 
many aspects. It tends to bring in its purview the railway passengers, and I find it 
proposes to strengthen the already strong provisions under section 12 of the Act. Mr. 
Minister, your section 12 has provisions more stringent and stronger than the material 
law. The only thing missing in section 12 is accountability. Your Head Constable

we have one accident each day, and I am told that we are almost graduating to two 
accidents a day. When an accident takes place, wherefrom do the rescue team

have neither the equipment nor the training to conduct those operations. Inside, we 
have the railway passengers who are shrieking to be rescued and they believe that they 
are bound to die, and outside, we have the railway employees who are busy with the 
gas cutters trying to save the human life, and one is unable to reach the other. My 
suggestion to you, Mr. Minister, is that only if you could use this Railway

famous dichotomy between the GRPF and the RPF. It was discussed here, and

police forces is the inter-personal relationship that a police force must have, and,

intensive manner. I am sure, the hon. Minister will look into this.

behaviour of the CISF with passengers earlier, but now, I feel that the CISF,
